paragraphs: There was once an old woman who earned a meagre living running errands and doing similar jobs for the farmers’ wives around her village. She earned very little, but with a plate of meat at one house and a cup of tea at another, she somehow managed to get by. She always looked as cheerful as if she lacked nothing in the world.
Well, one summer evening, as she trotted homewards, she came across a big black pot lying beside the road.

“Now that,” she said, stopping to look at it, “would be just the thing for me, if I had anything to put in it! But who can have left it here?” She looked around, as though its owner must be somewhere nearby. But she could see no one.
“Perhaps it has a hole in it,” she said thoughtfully:

“Yes, that’ll be why they’ve left it lying here, dear. But it would do nicely for a flower to put in the window. I think I’ll take it home anyway.” She bent her stiff old back and lifted the lid to look inside.
“Mercy me!” she cried, jumping back to the other side of the road. “Why, it’s full right to the brim with gold COINS!!”

For a while she could do nothing but walk round and round her treasure, admiring the yellow gold and marvelling at her good luck. About every two minutes she said to herself, “Well, I do feel rich and grand!” But soon she began wondering how best to take it home. She could see no way except to fasten one end of her shawl to it and drag it behind her along the road.

“It’ll certainly be dark soon,” she said to herself, “and people won’t see what I’m bringing home. Then I’ll have the whole night to myself to think what to do with it. I could buy a grand house and everything, and live like the Queen herself. I wouldn’t do a stroke of work all day, just sit by the fire with a cup of tea. Or perhaps I’ll give it to the priest to keep for me and take a coin whenever I want one. Or perhaps I’ll bury it in a hole at the bottom of the garden and put a little on the mantelpiece, between the china teapot and the spoons, for decoration. Ah! I feel so grand, I hardly know myself!”
By now she was already rather tired from dragging such a heavy weight behind her. She stopped to rest for a minute, turning to make sure her treasure was safe.
But when she looked, it was no longer a pot of gold at all. It was a great lump of shining silver!

She stared, rubbed her eyes, and stared again. But she could not make it look like anything except a great lump of silver. “I’d have sworn it was a pot of gold,” she said at last, “but I suppose I must have been dreaming. Yes, now, that’s a change for the better. It’ll be much less trouble to look after and not so easily stolen. Those gold coins would have been a terrible bother to keep safe. Yes, I’m well rid of them. And with my lovely lump, I’m as rich as rich—!”
She set off home again, cheerfully planning all the grand things she would do with her money. Before very long, however, she grew tired again and stopped once more to rest for a minute or two.

Again she turned to look at her treasure, and the moment she saw it, she cried out in astonishment. “Oh, my!” she said. “Now it’s a lump of iron! Well, that beats everything, and it’s so convenient! I can sell it easily, so easily, and get lots of pennies for it. Yes, dear, it’s much handier than all that gold and silver, which would have kept me awake at night thinking the neighbours were robbing me. And it’s a very good thing to keep in a house. You never know what you might use it for. And it’ll sell—yes, for a great deal. Rich? I’ll be rolling in it!”
On she trotted, chuckling to herself about her good luck, until she glanced over her shoulder, “just to make sure it’s still there”, as she said to herself.

“Oh, my!” she cried as soon as she saw it. “Why, it’s gone and turned itself into a great stone this time! Now, how could it have known I so badly needed something to hold my door open? Yes, isn’t that a good change! Dear me, it’s a fine thing to have such good luck.”
In a great hurry to see how the stone would look in its corner by her door, she trotted down the hill and stopped at the bottom beside her own little gate.

After unlatching it, she turned to unfasten her shawl from the stone. This time it seemed to be lying unchanged and peacefully on the path beside her. There was still plenty of light, and she could see it quite clearly as she bent her stiff back over it to untie the end of the shawl. Then, all of a sudden, it seemed to jump and squeal, and in a moment it grew as big as a great horse. It dropped down four lanky legs, shook out two long ears, flourished a tail, and went off kicking its feet into the air and laughing like a naughty, mocking boy.
The old woman stared after it until it was completely out of sight.
“WELL!” she said at last. “I really am the luckiest person around here! Imagine me seeing the Hedley Kow all to myself, and treating it so familiarly too! I can tell you, I feel so GRAND—”
She went into her cottage and sat down by the fire to think over her good luck.
